newsitem.title: USA: Digital Alpha systems hit by supply.
newsitem.headline: Digital Alpha systems hit by supply.

text.p: Digital Equipment Corp Chief Executive Robert Palmer said Thursday total sales of its Alpha systems grew by only one percent year-over-year in the second quarter due to supply contraints and slow growth in Europe.

"I view the slowdown in Alpha's growth as a short-term issue that will be resolved as we further strengthen our sales and marketing to bring our supply in-line with strong server demand," Palmer told reporters during a telephone conference call following the release of second quarter earnings.
Alpha system revenues rose 33 percent from the weak first quarter, he said.
Palmer said an order for high-end Alpha servers came in late in the quarter, but supply constraints prevented the company from shipping the products during the second quarter.

"Alpha revenues in the quarter were negatively impacted by a temporary supply shortage that led to a shipping shortfall of over $50 million as well as weak performance in Europe," Chief Financial Officer Vin Mullarkey said.
Mullarkey said publicity surrounding its negotiations in France and Germany to restructure operations there and a currency loss of around $20 million contributed to the slow growth in Europe.
"That tends to be a relatively public event in those countries...and this tends to impact and slow down our momentum," Mullarkey said.
The economy is also weak in France and Germany and business there is declining, offsetting growth in the United Kingdom and Italy, he said.
Mullarkey said Digital is still a "couple of quarters" away from reaching agreement on a restructuring plan in France and Germany and fully implementing it.
Palmer said Digital's semiconductor operations are on track to break even or turn a profit in 1998.

"Semiconductors operations...remain on track to be less of a drain on the corporate profitability," he said. "We've stated previously that we expected semiconductor operations to achieve breakeven status in 1998 and we're still on that track."

When asked if he still expected to beat analyst estimates of about $1.00 per share for the year as he told reporters following the annual meeting in November, Palmer said such forecasts were "reasonable."
"You just can't forecast, but the expectations seem to be reasonable to me," Palmer said.

Palmer said the company's sales force was "more stable" in the second quarter following a realignment to raise the number of customers covered directly to around 2,500 from 1,000 previously. The realignment unexpectedly impacted sales and contributed to the losses in the fourth and first quarters.
"But we're still one or two quarters away from realizing the full benefits of these changes," he said.
